bib.title: The p Value and the Base Rate Fallacy (Chapter 4, Statistics Done Wrong)

question: Why is a significant p value not the probability that a result is true, and how do base rates and multiple comparisons inflate false positives?
contributions: Worked examples of the base rate fallacy (drug screen, mammograms, gun survey)
Multiple comparisons, Bonferroni and Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate control

limits: Examples are illustrative worked arithmetic with assumed rates, not new data.
Bonferroni lowers power; BH controls average FDR but does not remove the base rate problem.
Chapter text gives year-less 1992/1980s survey figures via endnotes whose references are not in this excerpt; year of the book not printed in the chapter.
practices: Do not read p<0.05 as a 5% chance the result is false (Tips, p.53).
Use Bonferroni or Benjamini-Hochberg when testing many hypotheses (Tips, p.53).
Follow field-specific multiple-comparison practice such as in neuroimaging (Tips, p.53).
Use prior base-rate estimates to compute the probability a result is a false positive (Tips, p.53).
Prefer confidence intervals and effect sizes to significance testing (p.50-51).

terms.definition: the fraction of statistically significant results that are really false positives
Misinterpreting a low p value as the probability the result is a fluke, ignoring the base rate of true effects
the probability, under the assumption that there is no true effect or no true difference, of collecting data that shows a difference equal to or more extreme than what you actually observed
Particle physicists' name for multiple comparisons when searching many energies for an anomaly
with n comparisons, use significance criterion p < 0.05/n
Sort p values ascending, choose FDR q, m tests; find largest p with p <= iq/m; it and all smaller are significant
